units.title: Institutions
units.description: An analysis of the major social institutions—family, education, work, and religion—that organize social life and reproduce social structures.

lectures.title: Family and Education
lectures.description: This lecture examines how the family unit and educational systems function as primary sites of socialization and engines of social reproduction.

sessions.title: Family Forms
sessions.description: This session explores the diverse structures of family across cultures and history, ranging from nuclear to extended and blended families. You will learn to identify different kinship patterns and understand how these forms adapt to economic and social pressures. Understanding family diversity is a prerequisite for analyzing how modern social policies impact different household types.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the 'natural' image of the family. Most students arrive with a preconceived notion of the 'traditional' nuclear family—two parents and their children—as the historical and biological default. To break this, the lecture should begin by visually mapping out kinship on the whiteboard, starting not with the nuclear core, but with the 'Extended Family' as the primary historical baseline. Explain that for most of human history, the family was an economic unit of production (like a farm or a workshop) where grandparents, cousins, and multiple generations lived together because survival required a large, shared labor pool. This 'extended' structure wasn't just a choice; it was a functional necessity for risk-pooling and elder care before the existence of modern social safety nets.

Transition to the 'Nuclear Family' by linking it specifically to the Industrial Revolution. On the whiteboard, draw a clear line of causality: as work moved from the farm to the urban factory, families had to become geographically mobile. A large extended household is hard to move; a small nuclear unit is agile. Use this to illustrate the 'Functional Fit' theory—that family structures adapt to the needs of the economy. Point out a common misconception here: students often think the nuclear family is 'eroding' today, but it’s more accurate to say it was a specific adaptation to a specific industrial era that is now shifting again as our economy changes.

Introduce 'Blended' and 'Chosen' families as the modern evolution of these forms. Instead of presenting them as 'alternatives' or 'deviations' from the norm, frame them as flexible responses to rising divorce rates, longer life expectancies, and changing social values. Use a diagram to show how a 'Blended Family' creates complex webs of kinship that actually resemble the extended family's support network, just constructed through remarriage rather than bloodline. This helps students see that while the 'form' changes, the 'function' (emotional and economic support) remains the constant driver.

End the session with a brief reflective exercise. Ask students to categorize their own household according to these terms, but then push them to identify one 'economic pressure' (like the cost of housing or child care) that influences who they live with. This task is designed to move them from a personal 'feeling' about their family to a structural understanding of why their living arrangement exists. By the end of this session, students should see the family not as a static moral unit, but as a dynamic social institution that reshapes itself to survive the economic environment.

tasks: Contrast the nuclear family model with extended family structures in terms of economic support.
Identify how industrialization influenced the prevalence of different family forms.

sessions.title: Family Change
sessions.description: This session examines the shifting dynamics of family life, including rising divorce rates, cohabitation, and delayed marriage. You will gain an understanding of the sociological drivers behind these trends and how they reflect broader shifts in gender roles and individual autonomy. This knowledge helps you evaluate the 'crisis of the family' narrative through an objective sociological lens.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this session, we transition from the structural 'forms' of the family to the dynamic 'shifts' occurring in contemporary society. The primary goal is to deconstruct the 'crisis of the family' narrative—the common-sense panic that the family is disappearing—and replace it with a sociological understanding of institutional adaptation. We begin by visualizing a timeline on the whiteboard that marks the shift from the 'companionate marriage' of the mid-20th century to the 'individualized marriage' of today. Use this visual to argue that the family isn't dying; it is being redefined by autonomy and choice.

The core of our discussion centers on the economic and cultural drivers of delayed marriage. I will present the causal link between women’s increased labor force participation and the rising age of first marriage. It is crucial to frame this not as a rejection of family, but as a change in the 'marriage market' and life-course sequencing. On the whiteboard, map out the 'Economic Independence Effect' vs. the 'Income Effect'—the former allows women to leave or avoid unhappy unions, while the latter makes stable marriage more affordable but at a later stage. A common misconception here is that people are simply 'less committed' than they used to be; address this by explaining that the bar for a 'good' marriage has actually risen from mere economic survival to deep emotional fulfillment.

Next, we introduce Zygmunt Bauman’s concept of 'Liquid Love' to explain the rise of cohabitation and 'living apart together' (LAT) relationships. Use the metaphor of a 'contract vs. a bond' on the board. In a liquid modern world, individuals seek 'pure relationships'—connections entered into for their own sake and maintained only as long as both parties find sufficient satisfaction. This explains why divorce rates stabilized at a high level; it’s the result of a culture that prioritizes individual growth over institutional permanence. To make this concrete, ask the students to consider if a high divorce rate might actually be a sign of a society that values the quality of emotional life over the quantity of years spent in a miserable arrangement.

To bridge these theories into practice, I will prompt a reflection on how 'choice' creates anxiety. The practice task here—analyzing the link between work and marriage age—aims to reveal whether students can see the structural constraints behind what feels like a personal romantic choice. We will conclude by synthesizing these changes into a broader view of gender role evolution. If the family is less a site of economic production and more a site of emotional intimacy, the rigid gender roles of the past become dysfunctional. By the end of this session, students should see the 'modern family' not as a broken version of the past, but as a flexible response to the demands of an individualized, globalized world.

tasks: Analyze the relationship between women's labor force participation and changes in marriage age.
Explain the concept of 'liquid love' or individualized marriage in contemporary society.

sessions.title: Schooling and Credentials
sessions.description: This session investigates the transition from education as learning to education as a system of credentialing. You will learn about 'credential inflation' and the functionalist versus conflict perspectives on why we stay in school longer. This session clarifies how degrees serve as gatekeepers in the modern labor market.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by challenging the intuitive assumption that we attend school primarily to gain knowledge or specific technical skills. Start the whiteboard visualization by drawing two contrasting icons: a 'Lightbulb' representing human capital and learning, and a 'Stamp' representing the credential. Explain that while we often speak of education as the accumulation of skills (Human Capital Theory), sociologists are equally interested in the 'Credentialing' function—the way certificates and degrees act as gatekeepers to social status and employment, regardless of the actual content learned in the classroom.

Develop the concept of 'Credentialism' by tracing the historical inflation of degrees. On the board, create a timeline showing how a high school diploma once secured middle-class stability, whereas today, many entry-level positions require a Bachelor’s or even a Master’s degree to perform tasks that haven't changed in complexity. This is 'Credential Inflation.' Explain the logic of the 'rat race': as more people get degrees, the value of each individual degree drops, forcing people to stay in school longer just to remain competitive. Use the example of a receptionist position now requiring a four-year degree; it’s not that the job got harder, it’s that the labor market is using degrees as a sorting mechanism to filter out candidates efficiently.

Introduce the Theoretical Duel: Functionalism versus Conflict Theory. On the left side of the board, map the Functionalist view. Describe education here as a 'sorting machine' that identifies the most talented individuals and gives them the skills needed for complex roles in a modern, specialized economy. In this view, credentialing is a rational way to match talent with society's needs. On the right side, map the Conflict perspective. Here, credentialing is a tool of social exclusion. Explain that elite groups use specific degrees and 'prestige' schools to keep certain professions closed to the working class. The degree isn't just a sign of skill; it's a 'badge of membership' that proves you have the right cultural background and have been socialized in the 'correct' environments.

To prevent the misconception that these theories are mutually exclusive, facilitate a brief thought exercise. Ask the class to consider a surgeon versus a corporate manager. A surgeon needs the technical skill (Functionalism), but a manager might rely more on the status of their MBA (Conflict/Credentialism). This helps students see that education serves multiple masters simultaneously. Conclude by illustrating the 'Screening Effect.' The degree tells an employer that a student is disciplined and can follow rules for four years, even if they don't remember a single fact from their major. This shift from 'what you know' to 'what you have' is the central tension of the modern educational institution, setting the stage for our next discussion on how this system reproduces existing social inequalities.

tasks: Define credentialism and provide a real-world example of its effect on job requirements.
Compare the functionalist view of education (skill building) with the conflict view (status signaling).

sessions.title: Education and the Reproduction of Inequality
sessions.description: This session covers the 'hidden curriculum' and how schools often reinforce existing social hierarchies rather than providing a level playing field. You will be able to analyze how cultural capital and school funding mechanisms contribute to social reproduction. This is vital for understanding why educational attainment remains so closely tied to parental socioeconomic status.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start this final session by disrupting the common-sense notion that education is the 'great equalizer.' In a concept-first public lecture style, we begin by acknowledging that while we often view schools as meritocratic ladders, sociology asks us to look at the structural machinery beneath the rungs. The core goal is to understand 'social reproduction'—the process by which social inequality is transmitted from one generation to the next through the very institution meant to eliminate it.

Introduce the 'Hidden Curriculum' by asking students to think back to high school rules that had nothing to do with algebra or literature. On the whiteboard, map out the distinction between the formal curriculum (the textbook knowledge) and the hidden curriculum (the unwritten, unofficial lessons). Explain that this isn't just about 'manners'; it's about training different social classes for different roles in the labor market. For example, working-class schools might emphasize obedience and following rote instructions—skills for the factory floor or service sector—while elite schools emphasize autonomy, negotiation, and leadership—skills for the boardroom. The logic here is to show that schools don't just teach subjects; they teach 'dispositions' suited to one's likely class destination.

Connect this to Pierre Bourdieu’s concept of 'Cultural Capital.' Illustrate this on the board as a suitcase filled not with money, but with linguistic styles, tastes, and social navigation skills. Explain that schools are not neutral; they are biased toward the cultural capital of the upper and middle classes. When a student from a wealthy background enters a classroom, their way of speaking and their extracurricular experiences match the teacher’s expectations, creating a 'halo effect' that is often mistaken for innate intelligence. This prevents the common misconception that 'succeeding in school' is purely about hard work; it reveals that the 'game' is rigged in favor of those who already know the rules before they arrive.

Transition to the structural mechanism of 'Tracking' or 'Streaming.' Visualize a single entry point splitting into diverging paths. Explain how students are sorted into 'honors,' 'vocational,' or 'remedial' tracks, often based on standardized tests that are themselves culturally biased. The pedagogical point here is to demonstrate the 'self-fulfilling prophecy': once a student is tracked, the quality of instruction, the expectations of teachers, and the peer environment change fundamentally. Use this to bridge back to the idea of social reproduction—tracking ensures that the child of a professional remains on the path to becoming a professional, while the child of a laborer is funneled toward labor.

Conclude by discussing school funding as the material backbone of these inequalities. Illustrate the disparity between property-tax-funded suburban schools and underfunded urban districts. By the end of this session, students should see that the educational system functions less like a ladder and more like a filter. This sets the stage for their 'Sociological Autobiography' project, prompting them to reflect on their own educational journey: were they 'pushed' through the filter, or did the system's hidden curriculum and tracking mechanisms align perfectly with their existing cultural capital?

tasks: Identify three examples of the 'hidden curriculum' in a typical high school setting.
Explain how 'tracking' or 'streaming' within schools can lead to the reproduction of class inequality.

lectures.title: Work and Economy
lectures.description: This lecture analyzes the structural shifts in how goods and services are produced and the evolving nature of the relationship between employers and employees.

sessions.title: Labor Markets
sessions.description: This session introduces the concept of primary and secondary labor markets and the sociological factors that determine job quality. You will learn how social networks and structural barriers segment the workforce into 'good' and 'bad' jobs. This provides the foundation for understanding systemic disparities in employment outcomes.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the analytical heart of economic sociology. In this session, we are dismantling the myth that the labor market is a single, meritocratic open field. Instead, we visualize it as a 'Dual Labor Market.' On the whiteboard, draw a thick, vertical line dividing the board into two distinct sectors. This visual separation is crucial because students often assume that hard work leads to promotion regardless of the setting; we need to show that the setting itself—the structure—often dictates the ceiling. Label one side the 'Primary Market' and the other the 'Secondary Market.' Explain that these aren't just names for industries, but descriptions of structural conditions.

Start by detailing the 'Primary Market' characteristics: high wages, stability, clear career ladders, and benefits. Contrast this immediately with the 'Secondary Market,' characterized by low wages, job instability (the 'last hired, first fired' reality), and a lack of advancement opportunities. The core idea here is 'segmentation.' We aren't just looking at who has a job, but the quality of that job's infrastructure. To avoid the misconception that this is purely about individual education, emphasize that an overqualified worker in a secondary market job (like a PhD holder driving a gig-economy car) still experiences the structural disadvantages of that segment. Use the whiteboard to list three criteria for differentiation: the nature of the employment contract, the potential for wage growth, and the level of social protections.

Now, introduce the 'bridge' or 'barrier' between these worlds: Social Capital. Introduce Mark Granovetter’s concept of 'The Strength of Weak Ties.' Most students believe that close friends (strong ties) are the best source for jobs. Correct this by explaining that close friends likely share the same information and networks as the student. Visualize this on the board as a tight, closed circle of nodes. Then, draw a long, thin line reaching out to a distant node—a 'weak tie'—who inhabits a different social circle or labor market segment. This 'weak tie' is the bridge that provides information the student doesn't already have. This is the sociological explanation for why certain groups remain trapped in the secondary market; their networks are 'resource-poor' and lack the 'weak ties' to the primary sector.

Transition to a reflective practice moment. Ask students to think of the last job they found and whether it came from a 'strong tie' or a 'weak tie.' This exercise isn't just about personal history; it’s designed to reveal the invisible scaffolding of the economy. By mapping their own experiences, students begin to see how social networks serve as a form of 'informal stratification.' Conclude the session by emphasizing that labor market outcomes are not just products of individual human capital (skills and education) but are deeply influenced by where one is positioned within social structures and network architectures. This sets the stage for our next session on how these structures are being disrupted by the digital economy.

tasks: Distinguish between the primary and secondary labor markets using three criteria.
Explain how 'weak ties' in social networks can influence access to different labor market segments.

sessions.title: The Changing Workplace
sessions.description: This session discusses the shift from Fordism to post-Fordism, including the rise of the gig economy and precarious work. You will understand how automation and flexible specialization have transformed the daily experience of the worker. This session connects economic theory to the lived reality of contemporary professional life.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this session, we transition from the structural categorization of labor markets to the historical evolution of the workplace itself. Start by sketching a large, rigid factory assembly line on the whiteboard to represent 'Fordism.' Explain that this isn't just about making cars; it represents a specific social contract where mass production led to mass consumption. The core idea here is 'standardization'—of products, of work hours, and of life stages. Emphasize that in the Fordist era, the worker was an extension of the machine, performing repetitive tasks in exchange for relative job security and a living wage. This visual serves as the baseline for what work used to look like for much of the 20th century.

Now, erase the rigid lines and replace them with a network of fluid, disconnected icons to introduce 'Post-Fordism.' This shift is driven by technology and globalization, moving us toward 'flexible specialization.' Explain that the primary logic has changed from 'big and stable' to 'fast and lean.' Instead of one company owning the entire production process, work is now outsourced, automated, and fragmented. Highlight the importance of 'flexibility'—which sounds positive to a consumer (fast delivery, custom products) but often means 'instability' for the worker. This is where you introduce the term 'Precarity.' It is crucial to explain that precarity isn't just about low pay; it’s about the loss of predictability in one’s life, making it nearly impossible to plan for a mortgage, a family, or retirement.

To bridge theory to current reality, discuss the 'Gig Economy' as the ultimate expression of Post-Fordism. Use the example of a delivery app or ride-sharing platform to show how the 'workplace' has vanished into a digital interface. Address a common misconception here: learners often think the gig economy is just about 'extra cash' or 'being your own boss.' Correct this by pointing out that while the worker has the autonomy to choose their hours, the platform controls the algorithm and the pay rate, shifting all the risk (insurance, vehicle maintenance, lack of benefits) from the corporation to the individual. This is a form of 'digital Taylorism' where the surveillance of the assembly line is replaced by the surveillance of the app.

End the session with a reflective practice moment. Ask the students to consider how their own career aspirations—or the jobs they currently hold—fit into these models. Does their identity depend on their job, as it did in the Fordist era, or is their work just a series of 'gigs' that don't define who they are? This exercise is designed to reveal the psychological weight of the 'flexible' workplace. It helps learners see that the stress of modern professional life isn't a personal failure of time management, but a structural outcome of the shift to a post-Fordist, precarious economic landscape. This prepares them to understand the next session on how we use consumption to fill the identity gaps left by this unstable work environment.

tasks: Contrast the 'Fordist' assembly line model with the 'Post-Fordist' flexible specialization model.
Analyze the sociological implications of 'precarity' for worker identity and long-term planning.

sessions.title: Consumption
sessions.description: This session moves from production to consumption, examining how what we buy defines who we are in a consumer society. You will learn about 'conspicuous consumption' and how lifestyle choices act as markers of social class. Understanding consumption is key to grasping how modern identity is constructed through the market.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by pivoting from the 'work' aspect of the economy to the 'consumption' aspect. The central intuition to convey is that in a modern capitalist society, we don't just consume to survive; we consume to communicate. I’ll start by drawing a simple diagram on the board: a stick figure with an arrow pointing toward a product, but then a second, larger arrow pointing from that product back to society. This visual helps students realize that the market is a mirror. We aren't just buying 'things'; we are buying 'identities.' I’ll frame this as the shift from a production-based society, where your job defined you, to a consumption-based society, where your lifestyle choices serve as your primary social signature.

To ground this in theory, I will introduce Thorstein Veblen’s concept of 'Conspicuous Consumption.' I’ll write the term in bold and explain the underlying logic: if wealth is invisible, it cannot confer status. Therefore, individuals must 'waste' money on things that have high visibility but low practical utility—like designer logos or expensive watches—specifically to signal their position in the social hierarchy. A common misconception students have is that people do this simply because they are 'superficial.' I will challenge this by explaining that it is a rational response to a social structure that rewards status. To make this concrete, I’ll ask the students to think about 'digital conspicuous consumption'—how does a specific skin in a video game or a 'verified' badge on social media function exactly like Veblen’s silver spoons in the 19th century? This exercise reveals whether they understand that the medium changes, but the sociological impulse for status-signaling remains constant.

Next, we’ll transition to the concept of consumption as a marker of social class. I will draw a 'social map' on the whiteboard, plotting different types of consumption—not just by price, but by 'cultural capital.' This is where we move beyond just spending money to how we 'perform' our class through taste. I’ll explain that what we find 'distinguished' versus what we find 'vulgar' is often a way to maintain social boundaries. It’s important to emphasize that this isn't just about the rich looking down on the poor; it’s about how every group uses consumption to solidify their sense of belonging to a specific peer group. I will use the example of organic food or specific genres of indie music to show that 'high status' isn't always about being the most expensive; it's about being the most 'exclusive' or 'authentic' within a specific cultural logic.

Finally, we will address the darker side of this dynamic: consumption as a form of social control and integration. I’ll pose the question: if we are all busy trying to 'buy' our identities, are we less likely to challenge the structures that produce those goods? I will describe the idea of the 'consumer treadmill,' where the need to stay relevant through the latest goods keeps the workforce disciplined and compliant. I’ll end the session by having students discuss whether their latest 'identity' purchase actually felt like a free choice or a social requirement. This final reflection is designed to bridge the gap between personal feelings of 'liking a brand' and the structural reality of being integrated into a market system that demands constant participation.

tasks: Apply Veblen's concept of 'conspicuous consumption' to a modern luxury brand or digital good.
Discuss how consumerism can act as a form of social control or integration.

sessions.title: Capitalism and Globalization
sessions.description: This session looks at the macro-economic structure of global capitalism and the international division of labor. You will explore World Systems Theory and how the global economy links the prosperity of core nations to the labor of peripheral nations. This completes your understanding of how local institutions are nested within global economic forces.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this final session of the 'Work and Economy' lecture by shifting our lens from the local workplace to the global stage. The core objective is to dismantle the idea that national economies exist in isolation. I will start by drawing a large, interconnected web on the whiteboard, positioning different regions not as separate islands, but as nodes in a single, historical capitalist system. This visualization is crucial for helping students move past the common misconception that 'underdeveloped' nations are simply 'behind' or 'lazy'; instead, we will frame their economic status as a functional requirement of the global system’s current structure.

To ground this macro-theory, I will introduce Immanuel Wallerstein’s World Systems Theory. On the whiteboard, I will divide the world into three nested zones: the Core, the Periphery, and the Semi-Periphery. I'll explain the Core as the high-tech, capital-intensive 'management' sector of the planet—think the U.S., EU, and Japan—which focuses on services and high-end manufacturing. Opposite this, I will define the Periphery as the source of raw materials and low-wage labor. The most important takeaway here is the 'unequal exchange': how wealth is systematically siphoned from the periphery to the core, maintaining a cycle of dependency. Students often struggle with the 'Semi-Periphery,' so I will describe it as a buffer zone—nations like Brazil or India that exhibit traits of both, preventing a simple, volatile binary between the extreme rich and extreme poor.

Moving into the practice of mapping these flows, we will pause for a visualization exercise. I’ll ask the students to consider a common consumer object, like a smartphone, and we will collectively trace its components on the board: the rare earth minerals mined in the periphery, the assembly occurring in the semi-periphery, and the design/branding profits accumulating in the core. This exercise is designed to reveal the 'International Division of Labor'—the realization that your daily tools are physical manifestations of global inequality. This helps students bridge the gap between their personal consumption and the macro-economic structures we've been discussing.

Next, I will address the cultural dimension of this economic integration, often called 'McWorld' or 'Cultural Imperialism.' I’ll ask the students to identify local institutions—like a neighborhood cafe or a traditional marketplace—and discuss how globalization forces them to compete with standardized global entities. We will look at how the 'efficiency' of global capitalism often flattens cultural diversity, turning local traditions into commodities. This leads to a discussion on the tension between global homogenization and local resistance, ensuring students understand that globalization is not just a flow of money, but a flow of power and meaning.

Finally, I will conclude by discussing the 'Precarity of the Global.' I’ll explain how the mobility of capital (the ability for a factory to move overnight to a cheaper country) creates a 'race to the bottom' for labor rights worldwide. The lesson ends by challenging the students to think about the future: If the world system relies on this hierarchy, can 'development' ever truly be universal, or does the system require someone to stay at the bottom? This provocative question prepares them for the final unit on social change and movements.

tasks: Map the flow of capital and resources between 'core', 'semi-periphery', and 'periphery' nations.
Identify one way globalization has influenced local cultural institutions (e.g., fast food or media).

lectures.title: Religion, Media, and Health
lectures.description: This lecture examines how the 'softer' institutions of religion, media, and medicine shape our beliefs, perceptions, and physical well-being.

sessions.title: Religion and Society
sessions.description: This session defines religion as a social institution and examines its role in providing social cohesion and meaning. You will learn Durkheim’s concepts of the 'sacred' and the 'profane' and how collective effervescence builds community. This helps you look past individual faith to see religion’s structural function in society.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by de-centering the personal theological aspects of religion to focus on its role as a fundamental social institution. The goal is to move the student from thinking about 'what people believe' to 'what religion does' for a social group. I will start by drawing a large circle on the whiteboard labeled 'Society' and placing a smaller circle inside labeled 'Religion.' The lecture opens by defining religion sociologically: not as a matter of truth or falsehood, but as a system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things which unite into one single moral community. This shift is crucial because it prevents the session from devolving into a debate about specific deities and instead focuses on the structural 'glue' that holds groups together.

To build the core intuition, I will introduce Émile Durkheim’s distinction between the 'Sacred' and the 'Profane.' On the whiteboard, I'll draw a sharp dividing line. I'll explain the 'Sacred' as things set apart as extraordinary, inspiring awe and reverence, while the 'Profane' represents the mundane, everyday elements of life. To prevent the misconception that the 'sacred' is only found in churches or temples, I will use secular examples like the National Flag or a family heirloom. By showing how a piece of colored cloth (the flag) becomes 'sacred' through collective treatment, students realize that the sanctity is a social assignment, not an inherent property of the object itself.

Next, I will introduce 'Collective Effervescence,' a concept that explains the 'feeling' of being part of something bigger than oneself. I’ll describe this as the high-energy pulse one feels in a stadium during a winning goal or at a massive protest. On the board, I will illustrate this as a feedback loop: individual energy feeding into a group, which then radiates back to the individual, creating a sense of shared identity. This helps students understand that religious rituals are social technologies designed to renew the group's bond. A quick practice moment here asks students to identify a 'secular ritual'—like a graduation ceremony or a concert—and explain how it creates a boundary between the sacred event and the profane commute to the venue.

Finally, we will transition to the major theoretical tension of the lecture: Functionalism vs. Conflict Theory. I will map these out as two different lenses. For the Functionalist perspective, I’ll draw a web, showing how religion provides social support, purpose, and control. Then, contrasting this, I’ll introduce the Conflict perspective, specifically Marx’s 'opium of the people.' I’ll explain that while religion provides comfort, it can also justify inequality and discourage social change by promising rewards in the afterlife. The session concludes by challenging the students to hold both views at once: religion is simultaneously a source of profound community and a potential tool for maintaining the status quo, setting the stage for our next discussion on secularization.

tasks: Define the 'sacred' and the 'profane' with examples from non-religious social settings.
Compare the functionalist (integration) and conflict (opium of the people) views of religion.

sessions.title: Secularization
sessions.description: This session investigates the secularization thesis and the counter-arguments regarding the persistence of religious belief in the modern world. You will analyze how modernization affects religious authority and the rise of 'spiritual but not religious' identities. This session prepares you to discuss the role of faith in a scientific and pluralistic age.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing a central paradox in modern sociology: why, in an age of unprecedented scientific advancement, does religion continue to shape public life? This session tackles the 'Secularization Thesis.' On the whiteboard, I want to start with a downward-sloping line representing the traditional 20th-century view that modernization—scientific rationalism, urban living, and state-run welfare—inevitably leads to the decline of religious influence. We must emphasize that secularization isn't just about 'people stop praying'; it’s about 'differentiation,' where institutions like education and law split away from religious authority. The key takeaway here is that secularization describes a shift in power from the pulpit to the laboratory and the courtroom.

To prevent the common misconception that religion is simply 'dying,' we pivot to the counter-arguments and the complexities of the modern landscape. On the board, draw a cross-axis comparing 'Religious Belonging' (membership) with 'Religious Believing' (personal conviction). This helps students visualize Grace Davie’s concept of 'believing without belonging.' We will discuss how individuals in post-industrial societies often reject formal church structures but maintain intense personal spiritualities. This leads into the 'Spiritual But Not Religious' (SBRN) phenomenon, which I’ll frame not as a loss of faith, but as a shift toward individual autonomy and the 'privatization' of the sacred. 

Next, we introduce 'Religious Pluralism' as a direct challenge to the idea that science kills faith. I’ll use a marketplace metaphor on the whiteboard—the 'Religious Market Model.' Explain that when a society offers many competing religious options (as in the U.S.), religion actually thrives because organizations must 'compete' for followers by being more responsive to their needs. This is a critical moment for a practice exercise: ask students to identify one piece of evidence for secularization (e.g., declining church attendance) and one against it (e.g., the rise of mega-churches or political religious movements). This reveals if they understand that secularization is a multi-dimensional process, not a binary switch.

Finally, we wrap up by examining the social stability implications of pluralism. I’ll draw a diagram showing a 'sacred canopy' that has been fragmented. We discuss the tension: does having many religions lead to social friction, or does it foster a new kind of 'civil religion' where shared national values replace specific dogmas? The goal is to move the student from a simplistic 'science vs. religion' debate to a sophisticated understanding of how faith adapts to a scientific age. This transition sets the stage for the next session on media, which functions as a new type of 'sacred' authority in contemporary life.

tasks: Explain the secularization thesis and identify one piece of evidence for and against it.
Describe the concept of 'religious pluralism' and its impact on social stability.

sessions.title: Media and Technology
sessions.description: This session analyzes the media as a 'fourth estate' and a tool for social construction. You will learn about media concentration, the digital divide, and how algorithms shape our perception of social reality. This knowledge is crucial for navigating the modern information landscape as a critical citizen.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common-sense notion that media is a neutral mirror reflecting reality. I want to frame the media as the 'Fourth Estate'—not just a source of information, but a powerful social institution that constructs our shared social reality. Begin the whiteboard session by drawing a funnel. At the top, place the vast array of human events; at the bottom, the narrow stream of 'news' or 'content' that reaches the user. This visualization immediately prompts the question: Who controls the filter? This sets the stage for a concept-first exploration of social constructionism through a technological lens.

Introduce the concept of 'Media Consolidation' by mapping out a handful of corporate logos that own the vast majority of outlets. Explain the structural logic here: when a few conglomerates control the narrative, the 'marketplace of ideas' shrinks. The danger for students to grasp isn't necessarily overt propaganda, but 'agenda-setting'—the power of the media to tell us not what to think, but what to think *about*. Illustrate this by showing how certain social issues (like corporate malfeasance) might be de-emphasized compared to sensationalist celebrity news because of the underlying profit motives of the parent companies. We need to debunk the myth that 'more channels' automatically equals 'more perspectives.'

Transition to the 'Digital Divide,' but move beyond the basic 'haves vs. have-nots' binary of internet access. On the whiteboard, create a tripartite model of the divide: Access (the hardware), Literacy (the ability to parse truth from fiction), and Social Capital (how one uses the tool for advancement). Use the example of two students with the same laptop: one uses it for algorithmic doom-scrolling, while the other uses it to network with mentors and learn coding. This clarifies that technology often reinforces existing social stratifications rather than magically erasing them. This is a crucial moment to address a common misconception: that Gen Z 'digital natives' are inherently media literate. Remind the students that being able to use an interface is not the same as understanding the sociology of the algorithm.

Conclude by dissecting the 'Algorithm' as a sociological agent. Describe algorithms not as neutral code, but as 'encoded ideologies' designed to maximize engagement, often through the creation of echo chambers. Draw a feedback loop on the board showing how user data feeds an algorithm, which then narrows the user's worldview, which in turn reinforces their existing biases. This final beat should empower students to see their digital environment as a curated space. The goal is to transform them from passive consumers into critical citizens who recognize that their 'personal' feed is a structural product designed for specific institutional ends.

tasks: Explain how 'media consolidation' can limit the diversity of social viewpoints.
Analyze the 'digital divide' not just as a matter of access, but as a matter of digital literacy and capital.

sessions.title: Health Disparities
sessions.description: This session explores the social determinants of health and the 'medicalization' of social problems. You will learn why life expectancy and health outcomes vary so significantly by class, race, and geography. This session bridges the gap between individual biology and the structural 'causes of the causes' of illness.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by challenging the biological reductionism that often dominates our understanding of health. While people often think of illness as a purely physical or genetic event, this session shifts the focus to the 'social determinants of health.' I will start by sketching a ladder on the whiteboard to represent the social gradient. The core idea here is that health is not a binary—sick or well—but a spectrum that maps almost perfectly onto social class. We need to explain that while an individual’s choice to smoke or exercise matters, the 'causes of the causes' (like housing quality, stress levels, and food deserts) create the structural environment where those choices are made. The most important takeaway is that your zip code is often a more accurate predictor of your life expectancy than your genetic code.

Moving into the concept of 'Medicalization,' I will illustrate how the boundaries of medicine are socially constructed and constantly expanding. I'll use the whiteboard to create a timeline, showing how behaviors once viewed through a moral or religious lens—such as alcoholism (seen as a sin) or hyperactivity (seen as a lack of discipline)—have been redefined as medical pathologies. This is a critical transition because it shows how the medical institution gains social control. We must be careful to note that medicalization isn't necessarily 'bad'—it can reduce stigma—but it also individualizes social problems. For instance, if we treat a child's inability to sit still solely as a chemical imbalance (ADHD) rather than questioning the rigid structure of a 6-hour school day, we are using medicine to bypass a sociological critique of the environment.

To bridge these concepts, we will engage in a practice moment where students identify 'moral-to-medical' shifts. I will prompt them to think about 'burnout' or 'shyness' (Social Anxiety Disorder). This exercise is designed to reveal how the pharmaceutical industry and professional authorities can expand their market by labeling common human variations as 'conditions.' This helps students see that medicine is not just a neutral science, but a powerful institution that defines what is 'normal' and 'abnormal' in a given society.

Finally, we will synthesize these ideas by looking at the 'weathering' hypothesis and the cumulative impact of structural inequality on the body. Using a diagram of 'Chronic Stressors,' I will explain how the persistent experience of racism or poverty leads to physiological wear and tear (allostatic load). This allows us to explain why, even when controlling for income, certain racial groups experience higher rates of maternal mortality or hypertension. We wrap up by reinforcing that 'Health Disparities' are not accidental; they are the biological embodiment of social hierarchy. This prepares the students for their final project by giving them the tools to analyze how their own family’s health history might have been shaped by the economic and social structures of their time.

tasks: Define 'medicalization' and provide an example of a behavior that was once seen as a moral issue but is now seen as a medical one.
Use the 'social gradient in health' to explain why wealth correlates so strongly with longevity.
